rationale: Chomp (McGill) is a small, compute-bound recursive game-tree search with no static profile metadata, so the weighting favors low-risk, low-overhead passes that still disrupt static analysis: SUB gets high runtime/size weights because arithmetic substitution is nearly free and adds real diversity to the bit-manipulation-heavy search kernel; SPLIT is favored similarly since block splitting composes cheaply with other passes; FLA and BCF are kept at moderate security weights with reduced runtime weights because flattening and bogus control flow impose disproportionate overhead on tight recursive loops that dominate this benchmark's execution, so they should trigger only on functions whose features strongly indicate security payoff; IBR sits in the middle, obscuring the branch-heavy game-tree control flow at acceptable cost; ICALL and IGV are modestly weighted since chomp is direct-call and direct-global dominated, so indirect-call/global rewrites yield limited gain and carry correctness risk (varargs, function-pointer signatures) that outweighs their benefit on this workload.
